questions.title: Why does the partition function cancel out in the DPO derivation of Eq. (5)?
questions.question_body: In Section 4 the authors derive Eq. (5) by substituting the reparameterized reward (Eq. (4)) into the Bradley‑Terry preference model (Eq. (1)). They claim that the unknown partition function \(Z(x)\) disappears, leaving a preference probability that depends only on the ratios \(\pi^*(y\mid x)/\pi_{ref}(y\mid x)\). I tried to do the algebra myself but keep getting an extra \(Z(x)\) term in the denominator. Could someone walk through the derivation step‑by‑step and explain why \(Z(x)\) cancels?
questions.context: I'm reading the Direct Preference Optimization paper and am stuck on the change‑of‑variables that leads to Eq. (5).

questions.title: What is the intuition behind the importance weight \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x, y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x, y_w))\) in the DPO gradient (Eq. 7)?
questions.question_body: The gradient of the DPO loss contains a factor \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x, y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x, y_w))\) which up‑weights examples where the current model ranks the dispreferred response higher than the preferred one. How does this weighting relate to the KL‑constraint \(\beta\) and why is it necessary for stability? Would removing this term be equivalent to an "unlikelihood" loss?
questions.context: Section 4 describes a mechanistic view of DPO updates; I want to understand why this particular weighting is crucial.

questions.title: How does DPO handle multiple preferred responses (i.e., ties or rankings beyond binary) under the Plackett‑Luce model?
questions.question_body: The paper focuses on binary preferences \(y_w \succ y_l\). If we have datasets with full rankings or ties, can we still use the same DPO loss, or do we need a different formulation? How would Eq. (6) change for a Plackett‑Luce likelihood over >2 items?
questions.context: I'm interested in extending DPO to richer preference annotations.

questions.title: Why is a reference policy \(\pi_{ref}\) required in DPO and what are practical ways to obtain it when no SFT model exists?
questions.question_body: The algorithm assumes a reference distribution \(\pi_{ref}\) (typically the SFT model). The authors mention initializing \(\pi_{ref}\) by maximizing likelihood of preferred completions when SFT is unavailable. How does this affect the KL‑constraint term and does it introduce bias? Are there alternative strategies for constructing a good reference policy?
questions.context: Section 4 discusses initializing \(\pi_{ref}\) but I’m unsure about its impact.

questions.title: Can DPO be interpreted as performing implicit reward learning, and if so, how does its learned reward compare to an explicit reward model trained with Eq. (2)?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 shows that any reward function in the BT equivalence class can be written as \(r(x,y)=\beta \log \frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}\). Does this mean that after training, we could extract an explicit reward function from \(\pi_θ\)? If so, would its performance on downstream tasks match that of a separately trained reward model, or are there systematic differences?
questions.context: I want to understand whether DPO truly eliminates the need for a separate reward model or merely hides it inside the policy.

questions.title: How does DPO’s KL‑conservativeness parameter \(\beta\) compare to PPO’s target KL or clipping parameter?
questions.question_body: Both DPO and PPO regularize deviation from the reference policy, but PPO uses a target KL or clipped objective while DPO directly multiplies log‑ratios by \(\beta\). Is there a principled way to map a desired KL budget to a specific \(β\) value? What are typical values used in practice and how sensitive is performance to this hyperparameter?
questions.context: Section 5 sweeps over several \(β\) values; I’d like guidance on choosing it.

questions.title: Why does Unlikelihood training without the DPO weighting lead to model degeneration?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that a naive version of DPO without the importance weight (i.e., just maximizing log π(y_w) – α log π(y_l)) can cause degeneration (Appendix Table X). What failure modes occur—e.g., mode collapse, loss of fluency—and how does the weighting term prevent them?
questions.context: Understanding why simple unlikelihood is insufficient.

questions.title: Is DPO compatible with transformer architectures that use tied token embeddings for logits and rewards?
questions.question_body: Many language models share embeddings between token output logits and any additional heads (e.g., a scalar reward head). Since DPO treats the policy logits directly as part of the loss, are there any architectural constraints or modifications needed when using tied embeddings? Does sharing affect the implicit reward definition?
questions.context: I want to implement DPO on a model where I cannot add a separate linear reward layer.

questions.title: How does DPO handle long generation sequences where computing \(\log π(y|x)\) exactly is infeasible?
questions.question_body: "In practice" language models generate autoregressively; computing a full sequence log‑probability requires summing over all timesteps. Does DPO require storing these log‑probs for both preferred and dispreferred completions during training? If so, what are memory implications for large batch sizes or long outputs, and are there tricks (e.g., caching or truncation) used in the experiments?

questions.<title>: What theoretical guarantees exist for DPO’s convergence to the optimal KL‑constrained policy?
questions.<question_body>: Theorem 1 shows representational equivalence, but does DPO have any convergence guarantees under stochastic gradient descent? For example, does optimizing Eq. (6) provably recover the same optimal policy as solving Eq. (3) with exact RL given enough data and steps? How do assumptions about data i.i.d. and preference noise affect this guarantee?
questions.<context>: I’m curious about formal properties beyond empirical results.
